processing: Orthodox tea from early summer leaf, rolled by hand or machine. It is generally taken further in oxidation than first flush, as is typical of second flush teas in the Darjeeling tradition.
harvest_season: From about the second week of May to late July, before the monsoon flush.
appearance_dry: Typically darker and more even than spring leaf, wiry with some lighter tips.
appearance_liquor: Clear amber to coppery, as is usual for second flush orthodox teas.
appearance_wet: Coppery brown leaf with a mix of tones.
taste_profile: Rounder, stronger and darker than spring tea, with a soft finish; sellers often use the word muscatel.

brewing.notes: General guidance for second flush orthodox tea. It can take hotter water than first flush, and a splash of milk is possible though rarely needed.

vintage_note: Sold by harvest year as the early summer crop, usually cheaper than first flush. Some drinkers rate it as the best of the year. It holds up a little better than spring tea, but it is still best within a year or two.
description:
Second flush is Nepal's early summer orthodox picking, from mid May to late July. By now the leaf has more strength, and the tea tastes more like what most people expect from black tea than the pale spring pick does.

Few details specific to this flush are recorded. Its class suggests fuller oxidation and a darker leaf.

In the cup, expect more body and colour. If you like the idea of Darjeeling but find first flush too light, this is the one to try; some experts in fact consider this flush the year's best.

Check the harvest year and district when buying. Tea picked later in July may run into the monsoon period, so ask for the picking date when a seller can give one.
history: Little is documented about this flush in its own right. It is part of the four-flush calendar of Nepal's orthodox hill tea, an industry whose first estate, at Ilam, dates to around 1863.
